meta.title: Who really said "Education is a progressive discovery of our own ignorance"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, it's really Will Durant — a remark from his eighties quoted in Time in 1965. But it's near-always reproduced with no source. Here's the documented record.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Education is a progressive discovery of our own ignorance'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Will Durant, quoted in Time (1965) — yet reproduced everywhere with no source and often mis-worded. The honest, sourced record.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Consistently credited to Durant, and consistent with a real remark he made late in life — captured in Time in 1965 as “Sixty years ago I knew everything; now I know nothing; education is a progressive discovery of our own ignorance.” But it is reproduced almost everywhere with no source, the exact Time article cited varies between references ↗, and it has never been tied to one of Durant’s own books — so we mark it attributed rather than verified.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Teachers: The Essence of the Centuries,” Time, 13 Aug 1965 (per Wikiquote)
A reported remark quoted in the press — not traced to a Durant book

source.excerpt: Sixty years ago I knew everything; now I know nothing; education is a progressive discovery of our own ignorance. We teach more by what we are than by what we teach.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced Will Durant quotes ↗, citing Time magazine, “Teachers: The Essence of the Centuries,” 13 August 1965.
The full remark — “…we teach more by what we are than by what we teach” — survives on aggregators like Quotefancy ↗, but with no source of its own.
Other references instead cite a different 1965 Time piece, “Books: The Great Gadfly,” 8 October 1965 ↗ — the precise article is unsettled.
Quote-mill pages such as Goodreads ↗ reproduce only the bare one-liner with no citation at all.
source.excerptNote: The famous one-liner is almost always clipped from this fuller reflection — the self-deprecating opening and the closing sentence are usually dropped.
source.rightsHolder: The Estate of Will Durant; the wording as published by Time Inc.
source.rightsNote: The earliest documented appearance of this wording is a Time magazine feature in 1965 — well after 1931 — so the specific phrasing is in copyright in the United States, held by Durant’s estate and, as published, by Time Inc. The Socratic idea is ancient and free; this crisp English formulation is not.

author.name: Will Durant
author.heading: About Will Durant
author.metaLine: 1885–1981 · American historian and philosopher; co-author of The Story of Civilization
author.bio: Will Durant was an American historian, philosopher and popularizer of ideas, best known for the eleven-volume The Story of Civilization written with his wife Ariel Durant. The couple won the 1968 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction, and Durant received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1977. A former seminarian and teacher, he made a career of distilling vast subjects into aphoristic prose — which is exactly why humble one-liners like this one attach so readily to his name.

misattribution.heading: Real quote, phantom source
misattribution.intro: This one isn’t pinned on the wrong person — it really is Durant. The problem is that it travels as an orphan: no source, often re-worded, and stripped of the sentences that give it meaning.

items.why: Goodreads, BrainyQuote, AZQuotes and their imitators all publish the bare line with no source, which is why it reads like a free-floating aphorism. The actual earliest record is a 1965 Time citation ↗ that almost none of them carry.
The line is severed from its opening — “Sixty years ago I knew everything; now I know nothing” — and its close, “we teach more by what we are than by what we teach,” preserved on Quotefancy ↗.
Countless posts render it “Education is the progressive discovery” rather than the “a” of the earliest citation — a small but telling sign of quote-mill copying.

misattribution.truthLine: It is Durant — a genuine late-life remark recorded in Time in 1965 ↗; the fault lies in sourceless, context-free circulation, not a mistaken author.

context.heading: Why it rings true for Durant
lead: The thought is really Socratic — the wise person is the one who knows how little they know — and Durant, who spent a lifetime summarizing all of human learning, was well placed to feel its force. In its fuller form the remark is a piece of autobiography: an old scholar reporting that six decades of study left him more aware of his ignorance, not less.

That is also why the line is such a magnet for misquotation. It is humble, quotable, and flattering to attach to a famous polymath — so it spreads faster than its source, shedding context and citation along the way.
